Key Research Thinking Patterns: Isotope-Resolved Metabolic Tracing: Utilizing stable isotope probing (SIP) with 15N-urea and NanoSIMS to distinguish direct substrate utilization from indirect metabolic exchange in oligotrophic marine systems.

Trait-Based Ecosystem Modeling: Integrating microbial functional traits (rrn copy number, genome size) derived from metagenomics into the Microbial-ENzyme Decomposition (MEND) model to predict terrestrial carbon fluxes under warming scenarios.

Phylogenomic Lineage Reconstruction: Employing GTDB markers, IQ-TREE, and core/pan-genome analysis to reclassify ammonia-oxidizing archaea (AOA) and map their global biogeography and evolutionary history.

Multi-Omics Network Analysis: Combining metatranscriptomics, GeoChip 5.0 microarrays, and Molecular Ecological Network (MEN) analysis to elucidate cross-domain communication and co-occurrence patterns in response to environmental stressors.
Summary Description: Wei Qin bridges microbial genomics with ecosystem biogeochemistry, linking single-cell metabolic potential to macro-scale carbon and nitrogen fluxes. Specializing in ammonia-oxidizing archaea (AOA) and terrestrial soil microbiomes, Qin employs stable isotope probing (SIP), NanoSIMS, and high-throughput metagenomics to resolve niche partitioning and quorum sensing mechanisms. By integrating microbial functional traits into the MEND ecosystem model, the research quantifies how climate warming alters litter decomposition and soil respiration. This work establishes a robust, trait-centric framework that connects genomic adaptations to global biogeochemical cycling, providing critical insights into ecosystem responses to environmental change.
